prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

We report the discovery of 14 quasars in the vicinity of HE2347-4342, one of the two quasars whose intergalactic HeII forest has been resolved with FUSE. By analysing the HI and the HeII opacity variations separately, no transverse proximity effect is detected near three foreground quasars of HE2347-4342: QSOJ23503-4328 (z=2.282, $\vartheta=3.59$ arcmin), QSOJ23500-4319 (z=2.302, $\vartheta=8.77$ arcmin) and QSOJ23495-4338 (z=2.690, $\vartheta=16.28$ arcmin). This is primarily due to line contamination and overdensities probably created by large-scale structure. By comparing the HI absorption and the corresponding HeII absorption, we estimated the fluctuating spectral shape of the extragalactic UV radiation field along this line of sight. We find that the UV spectral shape near HE2347-4342 and in the projected vicinity of the three foreground quasars is statistically harder than expected from UV background models dominated by quasars. In addition, we find three highly ionised metal line systems near the quasars. However, they do not yield further constraints on the shape of the ionising field. We conclude that the foreground quasars show a transverse proximity effect that is detectable as a local hardening of the UV radiation field, although the evidence is strongest for QSOJ23495-4338. Thus, the relative spectral hardness traces the proximity effect also in overdense regions prohibiting the traditional detection in the HI forest. Furthermore, we emphasise that softening of quasar radiation by radiative transfer in the intergalactic medium is important to understand the observed spectral shape variations. From the transverse proximity effect of QSOJ23495-4338 we obtain a lower limit on the quasar lifetime of ~25 Myr.

outputs.L2:
We present the identification of 14 quasars surrounding HE2347-4342, one of only two quasars for which FUSE has resolved the intergalactic He II forest. Separate examinations of the H I and He II opacity fluctuations reveal no conventional transverse proximity signature around three quasars foreground to HE2347-4342: QSOJ23503-4328 (\(z=2.282\), \(\vartheta=3.59\) arcmin), QSOJ23500-4319 (\(z=2.302\), \(\vartheta=8.77\) arcmin), and QSOJ23495-4338 (\(z=2.690\), \(\vartheta=16.28\) arcmin). The absence of such a signal is mainly attributable to contaminating absorption lines and to overdense regions likely associated with large-scale structure.

Using the relationship between H I absorption and its corresponding He II absorption, we inferred spatial fluctuations in the spectral shape of the extragalactic ultraviolet radiation field along this sightline. The UV spectrum near HE2347-4342, as well as close to the projected positions of all three foreground quasars, is statistically harder than predicted by quasar-dominated UV-background models. We also identify three strongly ionised metal-line systems in the neighborhoods of these quasars, although they provide no additional limits on the ionising spectrum.

We therefore infer that the foreground quasars produce a transverse proximity effect expressed through localized hardening of the UV radiation field, with the most compelling evidence found for QSOJ23495-4338. Relative spectral hardness can consequently reveal the proximity effect even within overdense environments where standard detection through the H I forest is prevented. We further stress that radiative-transfer-induced softening of quasar emission in the intergalactic medium must be considered when interpreting the observed variations in spectral shape. Finally, the transverse proximity signal associated with QSOJ23495-4338 implies a minimum quasar lifetime of approximately 25 Myr.
outputs.L3:
Researchers identified 14 quasars in the vicinity of HE2347-4342, a bright background quasar whose intergalactic He II absorption forest has been resolved using observations from the Far Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Explorer (FUSE). This configuration provides an opportunity to search for the transverse proximity effect—the influence of ionizing radiation from foreground quasars on gas intersected by the nearby line of sight to the background source.

No conventional transverse proximity effect, expressed as a clear reduction in either H I or He II absorption, was detected near the redshifts of three foreground quasars. The absence of such an opacity decrease appears to result primarily from contamination by overlapping absorption lines and from enhanced absorption associated with overdense large-scale structures surrounding the quasars. These environmental effects can obscure the expected increase in ionization.

Nevertheless, statistical analysis shows that the ultraviolet radiation field near HE2347-4342 and the three foreground quasars is harder than predicted by models in which quasars dominate the metagalactic UV background. This localized spectral hardening provides evidence for a transverse proximity effect even where high gas densities prevent a straightforward decrease in absorption opacity. The strongest indication is associated with the foreground quasar QSOJ23495-4338.

The inferred influence of QSOJ23495-4338 on the neighboring intergalactic medium implies that the quasar has been active for at least approximately 25 million years, allowing sufficient time for its radiation to reach the observed gas. At the same time, radiative-transfer effects can soften the ionizing spectrum as it propagates through the intergalactic medium. Such filtering must therefore be considered when interpreting spatial variations in the UV spectral shape and when using transverse proximity signatures to constrain quasar lifetimes.
outputs.L4:
The study investigated fluctuations in the ultraviolet background around the bright quasar HE2347-4342 by searching for foreground quasars close to its line of sight. A survey of the surrounding field identified 14 quasars whose radiation could influence the intergalactic gas probed by the H I and He II Lyα forests. The researchers compared spatial variations in H I and He II absorption, using their relative opacities as an indicator of the hardness of the local ionizing radiation field. This approach was intended to reveal transverse proximity effects, in which radiation from a foreground quasar ionizes gas intersected by the sightline to the more distant background quasar.

A conventional search based only on reduced H I absorption did not produce an unambiguous proximity-effect signal. Absorption from contaminants, together with enhanced gas density in the large-scale structures that host quasars, could increase the H I opacity and conceal the additional ionization expected near an active source. The separate H I and He II measurements, however, showed localized changes in spectral hardness near three foreground quasars. The strongest case was QSOJ23495-4338, where the He II absorption decreased relative to H I, indicating a harder ultraviolet spectrum consistent with illumination by the nearby quasar.

These findings show that the relative strength of H I and He II absorption can reveal transverse proximity effects even in overdense environments where the traditional H I signature is weak or absent. Because radiation from QSOJ23495-4338 must have had enough time to travel transversely to the sampled intergalactic gas, the detection also places a lower limit of approximately 25 million years on the quasar’s active lifetime, subject to assumptions about its emission history and angular radiation pattern. More broadly, the results demonstrate that spatial variations in ultraviolet spectral hardness provide a sensitive probe of quasar activity, ionizing-background fluctuations, and the three-dimensional structure of the intergalactic medium.
outputs.L5: Observations of **He II** absorption provide valuable insights into the ionization history of the intergalactic medium. The **FUSE** (Far Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Explorer) satellite enabled astronomers to study these features in the spectra of distant quasars with high sensitivity. **This** research helps reveal how ultraviolet radiation from early galaxies and active galactic nuclei influenced the distribution and evolution of matter throughout the universe.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract for a research paper on the transverse proximity effect around foreground quasars near HE2347-4342, including the H I/He II absorption analysis, UV spectral hardness, metal-line systems, and quasar lifetime constraints.
counterfactuals.output: We investigate the transverse proximity effect produced by foreground quasars near the line of sight to the \(z\simeq2.9\) quasar HE2347−4342. Combining high-resolution H I Ly\(\alpha\)-forest spectroscopy with far-ultraviolet measurements of He II Ly\(\alpha\) absorption, we reconstruct the spatial variation of the H I/He II column-density ratio, \(\eta=N_{\mathrm{He\,II}}/N_{\mathrm{H\,I}}\), as a probe of the metagalactic ultraviolet background. Regions near several foreground quasars exhibit reduced He II opacity and low \(\eta\), while showing a substantially weaker response in H I, consistent with localized enhancements in the hard, \(E>4\) ryd ionizing radiation field. We compare these signatures with metal-line absorption systems identified along the HE2347−4342 sightline. Their ionic ratios provide independent constraints on spectral hardness and help distinguish quasar illumination from changes in gas density, metallicity, or thermal state. The combined H I, He II, and metal-line analysis supports a highly inhomogeneous ultraviolet background shaped by discrete quasars and radiative-transfer effects during the late stages of He II reionization. The transverse separations and line-of-sight velocity offsets imply that the illuminating quasars must have remained active long enough for their radiation to reach the absorbing gas, yielding geometry-dependent, Myr-scale lower limits on individual quasar lifetimes. The diversity of the observed proximity signatures further indicates that anisotropic emission, episodic activity, and foreground absorption can strongly modulate the detectability of the transverse proximity effect.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the main findings of a study that discovered 14 quasars near HE2347-4342 and investigated how three foreground quasars affect the intergalactic H I and He II forests.
counterfactuals.output:
- A deep spectroscopic survey around the bright quasar HE2347-4342 identified 14 previously unknown quasars. Three lie in the foreground and pass within only a few proper megaparsecs of the HE2347-4342 sightline, making them useful probes of the transverse proximity effect.

- The foreground quasars produced little or no unambiguous enhancement of transmission in the H I Lyα forest. Density fluctuations and the already strong metagalactic H-ionizing background can mask their additional H I ionization.

- Their influence was much clearer in the He II forest. Near the foreground-quasar redshifts, the He II absorption weakened and the inferred He II/H I ratio, η, declined, indicating a locally harder ionizing spectrum. Thus, quasars can strongly alter helium ionization without creating an obvious H I proximity zone.

- The correspondence between quasar positions and hard-spectrum regions supports a spatially fluctuating ultraviolet background dominated locally by discrete quasars. It also implies that at least some quasars had been emitting for roughly the transverse light-travel time—of order millions to tens of millions of years—unless their radiation is strongly anisotropic.

Overall, the study found the He II forest to be a substantially more sensitive tracer than the H I forest of the transverse radiation field, activity history, and emission geometry of foreground quasars.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a concise astronomy journal abstract explaining why no traditional transverse proximity effect is seen near QSOJ23503-4328, QSOJ23500-4319, and QSOJ23495-4338, yet local hardening of the UV radiation field still provides evidence for it.
counterfactuals.output: We investigate the transverse proximity effect associated with the foreground quasars QSOJ23503−4328, QSOJ23500−4319, and QSOJ23495−4338. None produces the traditional signature of reduced H I Lyα absorption along the background sightline. This absence can be explained if the enhanced ionizing flux is offset by excess gas density in the quasars’ environments, while anisotropic emission, finite quasar lifetimes, and variability may further weaken the expected H I transmission enhancement. Nevertheless, near each quasar the inferred ultraviolet radiation field becomes locally harder, as expected when quasar photons supplement the softer metagalactic background and preferentially ionize high-ionization species. The spatial correspondence between these hard-spectrum regions and the foreground quasars therefore provides evidence for a transverse proximity effect even where no H I opacity deficit is detectable. These results show that spectral-hardness diagnostics can reveal quasar illumination that is masked in conventional Lyα transmission measurements.

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe how comparisons of H I and He II opacity along the HE2347-4342 sightline can reveal the spectral shape of the extragalactic UV background and constrain the lifetime of QSOJ23495-4338.
counterfactuals.output:
H I and He II respond to different parts of the ionizing background:

- H I is ionized by photons above 1 ryd (13.6 eV).
- He II requires photons above 4 ryd (54.4 eV), which are produced mainly by quasars and are much more sensitive to the hardness and spatial fluctuations of the UV background.

Along HE2347−4342, the H I Lyα forest can therefore be used primarily as a tracer of gas density. Comparing it with the co-spatial He II Lyα absorption gives the column-density ratio

\[
\eta=\frac{N_{\rm He\,II}}{N_{\rm H\,I}}
 \propto \frac{\Gamma_{\rm H\,I}}{\Gamma_{\rm He\,II}},
\]

or approximately \(\eta \simeq 4\,\tau_{\rm He\,II}/\tau_{\rm H\,I}\) for matched, optically thin absorption. Low \(\eta\), or unexpectedly high He II transmission at ordinary H I density, implies a hard spectrum rich in \(>4\)-ryd photons. High \(\eta\) implies a softer background, strong filtering, or incomplete He II reionization. Thus the opacity comparison separates genuine changes in ionization from simple density voids.

QSO J23495−4338 provides a local hard source near the sightline. A He II transmission enhancement or reduced \(\eta\) near its redshift—without a corresponding H I void—is interpreted as a transverse He II proximity effect. Its location and extent are governed by the quasar’s retarded light cone: the radiation must travel from the quasar to the gas intersected by the HE2347−4342 sightline. Consequently, detection of the effect requires the quasar to have been shining for at least

\[
t_{\rm Q} \gtrsim
\frac{\sqrt{R_\perp^2+R_\parallel^2}-R_\parallel}{c},
\]

with an additional allowance for the He II ionization-response time. For the measured geometry of QSO J23495−4338, this corresponds to a lifetime of order \(10^7\) yr, commonly interpreted as a lower limit of roughly a few \(10^7\) yr, about \(20\)–\(30\) Myr depending on the adopted systemic redshift and UV-background model.

The constraint is not completely unique: quasar beaming or obscuration, variability, redshift errors, density structure, and the unknown ambient He II-ionizing background can mimic or weaken the proximity signature.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a technical abstract reporting a search for foreground quasars around the FUSE He II quasar HE2347-4342, with redshifts and angular separations for the three key objects, discussion of overdensities and line contamination, and a lower lifetime limit of approximately 25 Myr.
counterfactuals.output: **Abstract —** We report a spectroscopic search for foreground quasars in the field of the FUSE He II Lyα-forest sightline HE 2347−4342 (\(z_{\rm em}\simeq2.89\)). Three relevant foreground active nuclei are identified at \(z=2.282\), 2.302, and 2.690, with angular separations of approximately \(3.5'\), \(5.0'\), and \(10.7'\), respectively. Comparison with the FUSE spectrum shows that the expected transverse He II proximity signatures are not simple voids: the two \(z\simeq2.3\) quasars lie in a pronounced concentration of H I absorbers, indicating a matter overdensity whose enhanced recombination absorption can partly mask the increased ionizing flux. The feature associated with the \(z=2.690\) quasar is likewise affected by local structure, while individual apparent transmission or absorption features must be treated cautiously because the FUSE band is contaminated by Galactic H\(_2\), metal lines, and intervening H I Lyman-series absorption. After accounting for these effects, the enhanced He II transmission near the foreground-quasar redshifts is consistent with transverse photoionization. The light-travel-time geometry, particularly for the \(z=2.690\) object, requires the quasar to have emitted ionizing radiation for at least \(\sim25\) Myr, providing a lower limit on its active lifetime.
